site.title: Octos — The Embeddable Agent Kernel
site.description: Octos is a Rust agent harness kernel you embed. It owns turns, context, memory, tools, model routing and multi-agent execution behind one protocol; your app owns the interface. Apache-2.0.

footer.brandDescription: An embeddable AI agent harness kernel, written in Rust. The app owns the product; Octos owns agent execution and runtime state.
footer.license: Open source under the Apache License 2.0.

hero.heading:
Your app owns the UI.
Octos owns the agent.
hero.description: A Rust agent harness kernel: turns, context, memory, tools, model routing, sandboxing and multi-agent execution, behind one protocol. Embed it as a crate, a C library, a mobile binding, or run it as a server.

items.title: Turns and sessions
items.description: Open, hydrate, fork, roll back and compact sessions. Start, steer and interrupt a turn. The runtime keeps the transcript, the execution state and the durable ordering — not your client.

items.title: Context that survives long work
items.description: Three compaction tiers, from pruning stale tool results to a full summarizing pass, with a token budget and preflight checks before each call.

items.title: Memory in three layers
items.description: Automatic episodes of past work, long-term notes and daily notes as markdown, and an entity bank the agent writes on purpose. Hybrid BM25 and vector recall.

items.title: One toolbox
items.description: 35 built-in tools — shell, file edits, patches, search, web, git, checks, delegation — plus memory, peer, research and MCP tools registered per session.

items.title: Any model, with a fallback
items.description: 19 providers behind one router: capability lanes, hedge racing, exponential retry and a per-provider circuit breaker that degrades and recovers on its own.

items.title: More than one agent
items.description: Blocking sub-agents inside a turn, peer agents with their own sessions and worktrees, swarm fan-out with a validator gate, and a durable fleet kernel for long plans.

items.title: Safe by default
items.description: Every session runs under a sandbox backend and a permission profile. Workspace-write is the default; full host access has to be asked for and granted.

items.title: Hooks at every step
items.description: Shell hooks at 11 lifecycle points. A before-hook that exits non-zero denies the action, and a failing hook is disabled by a circuit breaker instead of wedging the loop.

items.title: Work that keeps going
items.description: Goals, loops and monitors let a session continue on a schedule, on an event, or when a watcher sees a change — under a token budget that stops it.

architecture.label: Architecture
architecture.heading: A kernel with a protocol boundary
architecture.description: 38 crates in one Rust workspace. Above the line, your app renders and acts. Below it, the kernel executes turns and owns runtime state. The boundary is a protocol, not a function call — so the client can sit in the same process, on a socket, or on another machine.

protocol.label: Protocol
protocol.heading:
OUP — one boundary,
three transports
protocol.description: The Octos UI Protocol is JSON-RPC 2.0. A client opens a session, starts turns, answers approvals and replays what it missed. Features are negotiated per connection, and the server never advertises a capability the client did not ask for.

transports.name: WebSocket
transports.description: GET /api/ui-protocol/ws — the sole chat transport, origin-checked against your allowed origins.

transports.name: stdio
transports.description: octos serve --stdio speaks newline-delimited JSON: one object per line, stdout for protocol, stderr for logs.

transports.name: In-process
transports.description: Link the crate and dispatch directly, with no socket in between — the path mobile and desktop shells take.

protocol.code: // start a turn {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"req-turn-start","method":"turn/start", "params":{"session_id":"local:demo","turn_id":"<uuid>", "input":[{"kind":"text","text":"hello"}]}} // approve a tool call the agent asked about {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"req-approval","method":"approval/respond", "params":{"session_id":"local:demo","approval_id":"<uuid>", "decision":"approve"}} // resume after a disconnect {"stream":"events","seq":42}
protocol.note: Streaming arrives as notifications — message/delta, tool/started, tool/completed, context/compaction_started. Every durable event is written to the session ledger before it goes on the wire, so a client that reconnects with its last cursor gets an exact replay, and one that has fallen too far behind is told to re-hydrate instead of silently losing state.

embedding.label: Embedding
embedding.heading:
Link it, bind it,
or run it
embedding.description: Octos is a library first. Take the crates directly in a Rust app, cross the C ABI from anything else, generate mobile bindings, or run the binary and talk to it over the protocol.

targets.name: Rust
targets.description: Use the kernel crates directly and keep everything in one process.

targets.name: C ABI
targets.description: A committed octos.h with a small surface: create a runtime, run a task, read the last error.

targets.name: Mobile
targets.description: UniFFI generates Kotlin and Swift bindings — this is how the kernel ships inside an Android app.

targets.name: Python
targets.description: A native extension module for scripting, evaluation and backend glue.

targets.name: Browser
targets.description: Protocol and utility types for web clients; the kernel itself keeps running natively.

embedding.code: // C ABI #include "octos.h" OctosRuntime *rt = octos_runtime_new(config_json); char *out = octos_run_task(rt, "summarize ./README.md"); if (!out) fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", octos_last_error()); octos_string_free(out);

context.label: Context
context.heading:
Long work,
without losing the thread
context.description: A turn can run for hours and stay inside the window. The kernel accounts for the budget, prunes what no longer matters, and tells the client every time it does — so the UI can show what happened instead of quietly dropping history.

features.label: Tier 1
features.description: Prune stale and oversized tool results between iterations, keeping the prompt cache intact.

features.label: Tier 2
features.description: Hand the provider its own server-side clearing where the API supports it.

features.label: Tier 3
features.description: A full compacting pass — extractive by default, or an LLM summary — preserving named artifacts and invariants.

lifecycle.name: hydrate
lifecycle.description: Page a session back into a client with its cursor and typed snapshot.

lifecycle.name: fork
lifecycle.description: Branch a session, keeping the last user turns and dropping the parent's tool noise.

lifecycle.name: rollback
lifecycle.description: Drop the last N user turns as an append-only, idempotent marker.

lifecycle.name: compact
lifecycle.description: Run compaction on demand, or let the preflight check trigger it.

context.note: Pruned tool results become typed placeholders that keep their call ids, so the transcript stays valid. With context.lifecycle.v1 enabled, the client receives compaction_started, compaction_completed and normalization_reported, each carrying the ids, triggers and token counts before and after.

memory.label: Memory
memory.heading: It remembers, in three layers
memory.description: Memory is not one blob. Episodes are recorded for you, notes are yours to read and edit as plain markdown, and the entity bank is written by the agent on purpose — each retrieved differently.

layers.title: Episodic — automatic
layers.description: Every completed task is stored with its outcome, the files it touched and the decisions it made, in an embedded key-value store. The six most relevant past runs for this directory come back on recall.

layers.title: Long-term notes — markdown
layers.description: MEMORY.md plus daily notes, with stable entry ids, a backup for rollback and an injection budget so the prompt never fills with history. Capture, extraction and consolidation run in the background.

layers.title: Entity bank — on purpose
layers.description: save_memory and recall_memory write pages for the people, projects and systems that matter. One-line abstracts sit in the prompt; the full page is fetched only when needed.

toolSystem.label: Tools
toolSystem.heading: One toolbox, one policy
toolSystem.description: Tools are Rust implementations with JSON schemas, admitted by a permission policy and executed inside the sandbox. Each declares whether it is safe to run in parallel, so a batch of reads fans out while writes stay in call order.

tiers.label: built-in tools
tiers.description: Registered with the permission-aware builtin registry.

tiers.label: concurrency classes
tiers.description: Safe tools run in parallel; exclusive ones run serially, and mixed batches are reassembled in order.

tiers.label: tool source files
tiers.description: Plus MCP tools and plugin tools discovered at runtime.

providers.label: Models
providers.heading: Nineteen providers, one router
providers.description: Route by provider/model, or by capability lane and let the router pick. Retries back off, failover walks an ordered chain with a per-provider circuit breaker, and hedging can race two providers and take the winner. Local and self-hosted servers are first-class: no key, no cloud.

agents.label: Multi-agent
agents.heading:
Sub-agents, peers,
and a durable fleet
agents.description: Not every parallel job is the same shape. A sub-agent is part of your turn. A peer is a colleague with its own session. A fleet worker is a closed executor working through a durable plan.

modes.name: Sub-agents
modes.summary: A restricted child inside the parent's turn. The parent blocks and gets one result back.
points: Inherits the workspace, tool policy and sandbox
Cannot re-delegate, spawn or message the user
Depth capped at two, with a typed budget error
spawn_agent is the background sibling of delegate

modes.name: Peer agents
modes.summary: A sovereign session with its own history, model lane and worktree, addressed by name.
points: Staged by the kernel, opened by the client
Fenced into its own git clone to avoid collisions
Coordinated through a file blackboard, gathered on demand

modes.name: Swarm and fleet
modes.summary: Supervised fan-out for one-shot work, and a durable kernel for plans that outlive a process.
points: Parallel, sequential, pipeline and fan-out topologies
Aggregate results pass a validator gate before they count
Workers get least-privilege grants: no network unless granted
A blocked worker escalates instead of waiting for a human

loops.label: Autonomy
loops.heading: Goals, loops and monitors
loops.description: A session does not have to wait for the next message. Set a goal, attach a loop, or point a monitor at something that changes — the kernel decides when the model needs to run again, and when it should stop.

stages.name: Goal
stages.description: An objective with a token budget, tracked in a durable ledger with its status and spend.

stages.name: Loop
stages.description: A stored prompt and mode that enqueues a continuation turn when it is due.

stages.name: Monitor
stages.description: A probe whose filtered output wakes the agent. Watching costs no tokens; only the wake-up does.

stages.name: Stop
stages.description: Budget exhaustion wraps up, a flood auto-pauses, and three empty continuations park the goal.

loops.note: Loop and monitor specs are persisted, so they re-arm after a restart; running child processes are not resurrected. Continuations are prioritized and de-duplicated, so a busy session does not stack up redundant turns.

security.label: Security
security.heading: Sandboxed, scoped, and asked first
security.description: The sandbox is the boundary, not the tool list. Every session runs under a backend appropriate to the platform, with a permission profile that says what the agent may touch.

layers.title: Six sandbox backends
layers.description: bwrap, Landlock, macOS sandbox-exec, Docker, Windows AppContainer, or none — chosen automatically per platform, and it warns when a fence is not enforced.

layers.title: Permission profiles
layers.description: Read-only, workspace-write or full host access. Workspace-write is the default; full access is refused unless the runtime mode allows it.

layers.title: Approvals that cannot be replayed
layers.description: A pending approval is bound to a SHA-256 digest of the exact arguments, to the room it came from and to the approvers snapshot; consumed approvals are rejected.

layers.title: Hooks with a circuit breaker
layers.description: Shell hooks at 11 lifecycle points. Exit non-zero before a tool call and it is denied; a hook that keeps failing is disabled rather than allowed to wedge the loop.

layers.title: Network off where it matters
layers.description: Cloud and tenant deployments default to network-denied. --no-network turns it off anywhere, and an explicit permission choice always wins.

layers.title: Loop and injection guards
layers.description: Three identical tool calls in a row abort the turn, an SSRF guard filters fetches, hook and probe environments are sanitized, and credentials are redacted from logs.

surfaces.label: Surfaces
surfaces.heading: The clients are separate
surfaces.description: Because the boundary is a protocol, a client is just a program that speaks it. These ship today, and yours can join them.

clients.name: Octoscode
clients.description: The terminal client. Provisions its own local runtime and speaks OUP over stdio.

clients.name: Octoscode Web
clients.description: The browser client over WebSocket, served by the binary alongside an admin dashboard.

clients.name: OctoSense
clients.description: The agent shell for desktop and phone, with the kernel embedded in the app.

clients.name: MCP
clients.description: Octos is both an MCP client and an MCP server, so other agents can call in and it can call out.

surfaces.channelsNote: The gateway is one surface among several: the same sessions can be reached from chat platforms, with history intact.

items.title: OctoSense — an agent shell
items.description: The kernel embedded in a Makepad shell for desktop and Android, where apps and cards are the interface and the agent reorganizes them around intent.

items.title: Octoscode — coding in the terminal
items.description: A terminal client for real work: turns you can steer and interrupt, sandboxed edits, checks, and sub-agents for the parts that fan out.

items.title: Your product
items.description: Give each customer an isolated agent with its own profile, memory and permissions, behind whatever interface you already ship.

items.title: Devices and robots
items.description: The kernel is small enough to live on the device, with safety tiers for actuation and a bridge to robotics stacks.

quickStart.label: Get Started
quickStart.heading: Run the kernel
quickStart.description: Build the binary, point a client at it, or link the crates. No Python runtime and no Docker required.
quickStart.code: # Build and install the CLI cargo install --path crates/octos-cli # First run: profile, provider, model octos init export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key # Talk to it in the terminal octos chat # Serve the protocol on 127.0.0.1:50080 octos serve # Or speak JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout octos serve --stdio # Expose the kernel to other agents over MCP octos mcp-serve # Check the environment octos doctor

items.question: Is Octos a framework, a library, or an app?
items.answer: A kernel you embed — closer to a library than a framework. It provides the execution loop, context, memory, tools and multi-agent runtime, and exposes them through a protocol. It does not provide a UI, and it does not ask you to structure your app around it.

items.question: What is OUP?
items.answer: The Octos UI Protocol: JSON-RPC 2.0 over WebSocket, stdio or an in-process dispatcher, with 105 methods and 50 notification types. Clients negotiate features at connect time, and durable events carry cursors so a client can reconnect and replay exactly what it missed.

items.question: How do I embed it in my app?
items.answer: Four ways: use the Rust crates directly, cross the C ABI with the committed header, generate Kotlin or Swift bindings through UniFFI for mobile, or use the Python wheel. If you would rather keep it out of process, run octos serve and speak the protocol.

items.question: Which models can it use?
items.answer: Nineteen providers are built in, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Vertex, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu, MiniMax, Qwen, Groq and OpenRouter, plus keyless local options through Ollama, vLLM and any OpenAI-compatible server. Routing, retry, failover and hedging are part of the kernel.

items.question: What stops an agent from doing damage?
items.answer: Sessions run inside a platform sandbox under a permission profile that defaults to workspace-write. Risky tool calls become approval requests bound to the exact arguments, hooks can deny actions outright, cloud deployments start with networking denied, and a doom-loop guard aborts a turn that repeats itself.

items.question: Can work continue when nobody is watching?
items.answer: Yes. A goal carries a token budget, loops schedule continuation turns, and monitors watch a file or process and wake the agent only when something changes — which costs no tokens while nothing happens. Budgets, flood control and a circuit breaker decide when it stops.

items.question: Is it open source?
items.answer: Yes, under the Apache License 2.0, on GitHub at octos-org/octos.
